analysis.one_liner: Lets states take over federal oil and gas permitting, fracking regulation, and royalty collection on federal land.
analysis.headline: The bill, with 5 cosponsors, never received a committee hearing or vote and died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The ONSHORE Act would have let states apply to take over the federal government's job of approving oil and gas drilling on federal land within their borders. It would have barred the Interior Department from enforcing any federal rules on fracking in states that have their own rules, exempted drilling on private surface land with 50% or less federal mineral ownership from federal environmental review, paid states their share of royalties directly, and required a review to open more of Alaska's National Petroleum Reserve to leasing. It was introduced in January 2018 and never moved past committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies drilling on federal land gain the most: permits would be issued by state agencies rather than the Bureau of Land Management, many operations on split-estate land would skip federal environmental review entirely, and federal fracking rules could not be enforced anywhere a state has its own fracking rules. Energy-producing state governments also gain a direct stream of royalty income and new permitting fee revenue.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil and gas producers and energy-producing states

how_it_helps.text: States could apply to receive exclusive authority to issue drilling permits (APDs) on federal land, with the Secretary required to approve or deny within 180 days, replacing federal processing with state processing.

The Interior Department would be barred from enforcing federal hydraulic fracturing rules in any state that has its own fracking regulations, and would defer to state rules on all fracking on federal land.

Oil and gas operations where the federal government owns 50% or less of the minerals would not need a Bureau of Land Management permit and would not count as a major federal action under the National Environmental Policy Act.
States could receive direct conveyance of their share of oil and gas royalties, bonuses, and rentals instead of federal disbursement, and could collect permitting fees for their own programs.
The Secretary would have to review the management plan for the National Petroleum Reserve-Alaska and make additional land there available for oil and gas leasing.

analysis.who_pays: The public that owns the federal minerals pays through reduced federal oversight: federal fracking rules would be unenforceable in states with their own rules, federal environmental review would disappear for split-estate drilling, and lease-sale protests would have to be resolved within 60 days. People living near federal drilling would rely solely on state regulators for protection.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers who own federal minerals and communities near drilling

drawbacks.text: Exempting split-estate operations (federal mineral share of 50% or less) from any federal environmental review removes the National Environmental Policy Act check on drilling that can affect federally owned minerals and nearby land.

Barring federal enforcement of fracking rules in any state with its own fracking regulations means the stringency of protection on federal land would vary by state, and the federal government could not set a floor.
Requiring the Secretary to resolve lease-sale protests within 60 days shortens the window to review objections before federal land is leased for drilling.

Supporters would acknowledge a federal cost: delegation is limited to states deemed 'at least as effective' and does not cover national parks, wildlife refuges, or wilderness, but once authority is delegated, resuming federal control requires finding a deficiency, notice, and a 30-day state response period, and a state can appeal any such determination in federal court.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated logic is cooperative federalism: states are closer to drilling activity and could process permits faster, and states would keep more of the royalty money directly. But the provisions go well beyond streamlined permitting — a blanket federal hands-off rule on fracking, a NEPA exemption for split-estate drilling, a 60-day deadline on lease protests, and expanded leasing in the National Petroleum Reserve-Alaska. The speed and revenue gains accrue mainly to drillers and producing states, while the federal backstop on public land and water protection would be reduced. For a reader wondering who wins, it is the industry that gets the permits, not the public that owns the land.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which never scheduled a hearing or vote, and it died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Senator John Barrasso introduced the ONSHORE Act on January 18, 2018, with Senators Hoeven, Enzi, Lee, and Hatch as original cosponsors.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources, the only action it ever received.
Five senators cosponsored the bill, four Republicans and one Democrat.
No further committee action, hearing, markup, or floor vote appears in the bill's action history through the end of the 115th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, federal oversight of fracking and drilling on federal land stayed as it was. The bill's target beneficiaries, oil and gas producers seeking faster state-run permitting and reduced federal environmental review, gained nothing, and no interest group was harmed by its death. Communities near federal drilling and users of public land are no worse off than before.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal oversight intact; industry gained nothing

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so the partisan shape of support is unknown; sponsorship was 4 Republicans and 1 Democrat among 5 cosponsors.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers on federal land
industries.note: The bill would hand drilling permit decisions to state agencies, exempt split-estate operations from NEPA review, and bar federal fracking enforcement in any state with its own rules, all of which shorten and lighten the review drillers face. The public that owns the minerals bears the reduced oversight, so the industry's gain runs against the public's interest here.

States would gain exclusive permitting authority, permitting fee revenue, and direct conveyance of their royalty share, giving them more money and control. How that serves the public depends on the state; it removes a federal backstop while adding state revenue.

industries.industry: Federal oil and gas inspection and royalty administration (Bureau of Land Management / Interior)
industries.note: The bill would strip the Interior Department of permitting authority, fracking enforcement, and fee collection in delegating states, and shield certain activities from its permitting entirely. Its loss is the public's check on drilling going away.
